messages:
owen: Quick sync — sketching a migration approach for service auth: sidecar proxies that mint per-request ephemeral creds vs a central token-broker service. looking for pros/cons we might have missed. TL;DR: want to reduce long-lived key surface and keep operator tokens minimal.

maya: high level: sidecar gives locality + no central hop, broker gives central audit and simpler rotation. tradeoffs on perf though.

liam: if we do sidecars, we need strict mTLS + identity bootstrapping. otherwise attackers can spoof and mint tokens.

darya: can we do hybrid? sidecars for low-latency intra-region calls, broker for cross-region or admin flows. fallback rules?

owen: hybrid seems plausible. my worry: complexity in routing & audit correlation. if both mint tokens, logs scatter. how do we attach operator trace id?

ben: attach a consistent provenance header at mint time, e.g. X-Redwood-Auth-Trace: <trace-id>. both sidecar and broker emit same format. that lets observability join logs.

maya: about scoping: broker can enforce strict org/project scoping centrally — sidecars will need local policy cache. cache invalidation becomes hard during org changes.

liam: right. we already saw cache-stale fallout in another service. solution: short TTL + push invalidation via control-plane pubsub. still some window of mismatch.

owen: performance numbers? estimated added P50 latency for broker hop ~5-10ms in-region, 30-80ms cross-region. sidecar zero extra hop but +2-4ms CPU to sign tokens. Does that match infra expectations?

darya: those are reasonable. but broker can also provide token reuse: issue short-lived tokens and a reuse cache to avoid minting spike. helps cold-start bursts.

ben: threat model: broker centralization reduces per-host secret sprawl but becomes high-value target. need HSM-backed signing keys and chunked trust so broker compromise doesn’t auto-escalate across tenants.

liam: can we design broker with tenant-scoped signing keys (KMS per-tenant) + key-wrapping so operator token only wraps delegation rights? adds cost but less blast radius.

maya: operationally, rotation is easier in broker (one place) but sidecar rotation requires rollout coordination. both need graceful fallback.

nowen: (typo) owen: question re RBAC: should token include explicit role claims or only actor id and let destination resolve roles? pros/cons?

darya: include minimal claims (actor id, tenant id, intent). destination should evaluate policy against actor and tenant to get roles — avoids token re-issuance on role changes.

ben: downside: more policy evals in hot path. but keeps tokens lean & immutable. also better for rapid role flips.

maya: agree. also add an optional ephemeral role claim for short-lived elevated ops, but require 2-step validation (broker + dst).

liam: example token payload sketch:

```
{
  "sub": "svc-ingest-processor",
  "tid": "org_42",
  "iat": 1670000000,
  "exp": 1670000060,
  "intent": "write:events",
  "prov_trace": "trace-abc123"
}
```

liam: note: no roles field. destination queries policy service with sub+tid to map roles.

owen: good sketch. next steps: 1) prototype sidecar mint + provenance header 2) design broker KMS-per-tenant POC 3) run threat model for both. volunteers?

maya: I can take the sidecar prototype. will make a small Rust binary and expose a local unix socket.

liam: I'll start the broker KMS design doc and cost estimates.

darya: I'll own the policy-eval perf tests and invalidation story.

ben: I'll run the threat modeling and HSM integration checklist.

security-bot: Deploy check: reminder — any prototype that handles creds must use staging KMS and be behind feature flag. Incident channel #incidents will be auto-subscribed.

owen: thanks team. will write up action items and a short RFC follow-up with the tradeoffs and a migration timeline. :thumbsup:
